It Wasn’t The Himalayas are warming and alarm is fading. by Keith Schneider September 10, 2026 September 10, 2026 Share this article: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Printed lists of the missing were fixed this month to the dry walls of Nepalese buildings not swept away by the boiling tower of mud and boulders so tall, and moving so fast, that it looked like an AI fake. It wasn’t of course. The Himalayas are warming and melting faster than almost anywhere else on the planet. Flash floods that wreck villages and kill people are common now. In 2014 Circle of Blue reported on the aftermath of a climate change flood that was even more deadly than the one last week. It inundated two river valleys, destroyed dams, wrecked 1,000 kilometers of highways, and killed 30,000 people in Uttarakhand, a Himalayan state in India. Unlike the Uttarakhand disaster, the Nepal catastrophe is distinguished both by the ferocity of the flood waters and the number of eye witnesses who recorded and posted images on global social media channels. For a moment, at least, the world took notice and sent assistance. Hopefully the attention won’t be temporary, which is a sad and an all-too-familiar feature of climate-related tragedies. Just as science forecasted three decades ago, Mother Earth is heating up rapidly now. Himalayan snow, ice, and permafrost are melting twice as fast today as they did at the start of the century. Yet while people and some governments, including the U.S., once expressed alarm, signed the Paris Climate Accord in 2015, and promoted low-carbon industrial responses like clean cars and renewable energy, that era has largely passed except in a handful of nations like China, Pakistan (solar installation) and Norway (EV car sales).
